activities.title: Find the claim with its reason
activities.instructions:
Original fictional letter. A resident writes to the town council about a proposal for a weekend farmers market in Riverside Park:

"The proposed weekend farmers market in Riverside Park. A market would bring lively crowds to a quiet corner of the park. Vendors should be allowed to sell fresh produce there every Saturday, because the surrounding streets have no shop that sells fresh vegetables. Some stallholders have already asked about a spot."

Your task: quote one sentence from the letter that is a claim-plus-reason, or state that none qualifies. Then, in the same response, explain in one or two sentences how the reason is meant to support the asserted position. Use only the supplied paragraph; do not invent new wording or facts.

Accepts a reasoned alternative if the learner argues another sentence also qualifies, provided both parts are present

activities.worked_solution:
Your quoted sentence and explanation of how its reason supports it

The intended sentence is: "Vendors should be allowed to sell fresh produce there every Saturday, because the surrounding streets have no shop that sells fresh vegetables." Its assertion — that vendors should be allowed to sell there — takes a position a reader could reject, for example by arguing the park is unsuitable or that a market would crowd out other users. The reason after "because" is meant to support that position: if no nearby shop sells fresh vegetables, the market fills a real gap, so allowing vendors serves a need. That link is itself challengeable — a reader could deny that the area lacks such a shop, or agree it does but still oppose Saturday trading — which is what makes the sentence a claim-plus-reason rather than a bare topic or claim. The opening sentence is only a topic phrase naming the proposal; the crowd sentence asserts something but gives no explicit reason; the stallholder sentence reports a fact without taking an arguable position. A no-qualifying-sentence answer is defensible only if justified against these actual sentences, and here the "because" sentence clearly fits. Accept an argued alternative only if it names both an assertion someone could deny and an explicit reason within the letter's actual wording.
